## Level 1: Legal baseline

- [ ] **CORE-AI-01** (MUST) Every AI component is listed. An AI inventory lists each model, its provider, purpose, inputs (health data or not), outputs, human oversight and AI Act role. Provider settings for retention and training are recorded.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-AI-02** (MUST) AI says it is AI, and not a clinician, from the first message. A chatbot, agent or AI character tells people from the first interaction that it is AI and not a doctor, nurse or therapist, in plain words, and repeats it when the topic turns to symptoms or treatment. Generated images and audio carry machine-readable marks.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-AI-03** (MUST) A general chatbot does not diagnose or advise treatment. Unless the product is qualified as a medical device for that purpose, its AI does not give a diagnosis, a risk score for a disease, a dose or a treatment change for an individual. It gives general information and points to a professional. The limits are tested with red-team prompts before each model change.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-AI-04** (MUST) AI providers do not keep or train on health data. Health data sent to an AI provider is covered by a processing agreement, zero or minimal retention, and no training on it. Health data of users is not used to train or fine-tune the maker's own models without a DPIA, an Art. 9 condition and, for research, approval.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-AI-05** (MUST) AI does not exploit illness, age or distress. AI features do not use manipulative techniques, or exploit vulnerability due to age, disability, illness or a difficult situation, to change what people do in a way that harms them (for example pushing purchases or stopping treatment).  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-CHD-01** (MUST) Products used by children also meet the CSEF core. When children use the product, it also meets the core rules of the Child-Safe EdTech Framework that fit it (age assurance, parental consent below the national age, design and communication rules), and records the CSEF check.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-COM-01** (MUST) People are told in plain words what happens to their health data. Before the first health data is collected, a short plain-language notice says what is collected, why, who receives it, where it is stored and for how long. The full privacy notice is one tap away.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-COM-02** (MUST) No dark patterns around consent, cancellation or worry. Consent, subscription and cancellation flows are neutral: equal buttons, no confirm-shaming, no fear-based messages about health to drive purchases, cancellation as easy as sign-up.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-COM-03** (MUST) Notifications do not reveal health on the lock screen. By default, notifications say nothing about a condition, medication or result ("Time for your check-in", not "Take your HIV medication"). People can choose more detail.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-01** (MUST) Health data is identified, including what other data reveals. The data inventory marks every field that is health, genetic or biometric data, and every field that reveals health when linked to a person: orders of medicines or health products, app use itself (using a diabetes app), step counts or sleep patterns that show a condition, appointments.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-02** (MUST) Each use of health data has an Art. 9 condition. For each purpose that uses health data, the record names both the Art. 6 legal basis and the Art. 9(2) condition (for example explicit consent, health or social care under professional secrecy, public health, research). Purposes that have no condition are not carried out.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-03** (MUST) A DPIA is done before launch and kept current. A data protection impact assessment covers the product before launch and is updated when features, processors or purposes change.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-04** (MUST) Explicit consent is separate, specific and easy to withdraw. Where consent is the Art. 9 condition, it is asked separately from the terms, for each purpose, with no pre-ticked box, and can be withdrawn in the app as easily as it was given. Refusing optional uses never blocks the core service.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-05** (MUST) Only the health data the purpose needs is collected. Each health field has a purpose that needs it. Optional fields are marked optional. Free-text fields are avoided where a choice list works. Raw sensor streams are reduced on the device when the purpose only needs a summary.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-06** (MUST) Retention periods are set and enforced. Every store of health data has a retention period and a job that deletes or anonymises data when it ends, including backups and processor copies. National rules for clinical records apply where they exist.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-07** (MUST) Every processor that receives health data has a contract and is listed. Each third party (hosting, analytics, support desk, AI provider, crash reporting) is listed with what it receives. Those that receive health data have a data processing agreement that covers it.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-08** (MUST) Transfers outside the EEA have a legal tool. Health data is stored in the EEA by default. Any transfer outside it (including support access and AI providers) rests on an adequacy decision or another Chapter V tool, documented with a transfer assessment.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-09** (MUST) People can see, export and delete their data. In the product, a person can see their health data, download it in a common machine-readable format and delete their account and data. Data from connected devices is part of the export.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-10** (MUST) No health data in logs, crash reports or debug output. Logs, crash reports, error trackers and debug output never contain health values, symptoms, diagnoses, medications or free text written by the person.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-12** (MUST) Health data on the device is encrypted. Health data stored on a phone, tablet or browser uses encrypted storage (Keychain, Keystore, encrypted databases). Plain localStorage, AsyncStorage, SharedPreferences or UserDefaults are not used for it.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-GOV-01** (MUST) Named people are responsible for data protection and safety. The product names who is responsible for data protection, security and (for devices) regulatory compliance. A data protection officer is appointed where health data is processed at large scale as a core activity.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-QUA-01** (MUST) The intended purpose is written down. The product has one written intended purpose: what it is for, for whom, and what it claims to do. The same text drives the store listing, the website, the onboarding screens and the qualification decision.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-QUA-02** (MUST) The medical device question is answered and recorded. Before launch, the maker decides whether the product, or any module of it, is medical device software (MDR), in vitro diagnostic software (IVDR), an Annex XVI product, or none of these, and records the reasons step by step against the MDCG 2019-11 decision trees. "Undecided" is not a launch state.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-QUA-03** (MUST) Claims match the qualification. Nothing the product or its maker says (store listing, website, adverts, onboarding, AI answers) claims a medical purpose the qualification does not cover: diagnosing, treating, monitoring a disease, predicting it, or calculating doses.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-SEC-01** (MUST) A security policy and a way to report vulnerabilities. The product has a published security contact and vulnerability disclosure policy, and a named person who handles reports.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-SEC-02** (MUST) All traffic is encrypted. All network traffic uses TLS. No endpoint uses plain http, except local development.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-SEC-03** (MUST) Access to health records needs strong authentication. Access to stored health data needs a login with protection against guessing. Accounts of health professionals and administrators use multi-factor authentication. Sessions on shared devices time out.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-SEC-04** (MUST) Breach and incident response is planned and rehearsed. A written plan says who decides, who tells the data protection authority within 72 hours, who tells affected people, and, where they apply, who reports to the national CSIRT (NIS2) and ENISA (CRA). It is rehearsed once a year.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-SEC-06** (MUST) No secrets in the code. API keys, private keys and passwords are never committed. They live in a secret store.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-TRK-01** (MUST) No advertising or tracking SDKs without consent, and none where health data is shown. Advertising, attribution and cross-app tracking SDKs are not loaded before consent, and never run on screens that collect or show health data. Product analytics, if used, is first-party or a processor bound by contract, without advertising identifiers.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-TRK-02** (MUST) Events sent to analytics do not reveal health. Event names and properties sent to any analytics or marketing tool do not contain or imply a condition, symptom, medication or result ("insulin_logged", "depression_test_done").  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-TRK-03** (MUST) No advertising based on health data. Health data, and data that reveals health, is never used to target, measure or sell advertising, inside or outside the product, and is not sold or shared with data brokers.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **R-DAT-01** (MUST) Research uses have a legal basis and approval. Each research use of health data has an Art. 6 basis, an Art. 9(2) condition (often (j) with national safeguards, or explicit consent), ethics approval where required, and a protocol. Research use is not hidden inside the terms of service.

## Level 2: Forward-compliant

- [ ] **CORE-ACC-01** (SHOULD) The product is accessible. The product meets WCAG 2.2 level AA (EN 301 549). Public sector bodies publish an accessibility statement. Health information is also offered in plain language.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-CHD-02** (MUST) Teenagers' confidential health topics stay confidential. Parent or guardian access to a teenager's data follows national law on consent and confidentiality for health care. Topics such as sexual health, mental health and substance use are not shown to parents by default where the teenager may consult on their own.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-DAT-11** (SHOULD) Analytics and research use pseudonymised data with keys kept apart. Product analytics and research extracts use random codes instead of identities. The key that links codes to people stays in a separate system with separate access. Recipients that cannot re-identify are named when the data is collected.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-GOV-02** (SHOULD) The manifest and the qualification are reviewed every year. hdsf.yaml, the qualification and the DPIA are reviewed at least once a year and after any major change.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-QUA-04** (SHOULD) The qualification is checked again when the product changes. A new feature, a new claim, a new AI model or a new user group triggers a recorded check of the qualification and the class. The check is part of the release checklist.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-SAF-01** (MUST) People can always find urgent help. Where people enter symptoms, talk about mental health or chat (with AI or people), the product shows how to get urgent help (112 and national lines) in one tap, and says the product is not an emergency service. Words that signal danger lead to that help, not to a generic answer.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-SAF-02** (SHOULD) Health content is reviewed by a qualified person and dated. Health information in the product is written or reviewed by a named, qualified professional, cites its sources and shows when it was last reviewed. Reviews happen at least yearly.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-SEC-05** (MUST) Components are listed and security updates are promised. The product keeps a software bill of materials, watches it for known vulnerabilities, and states how long it will receive security updates.  
      Evidence: 
- [ ] **CORE-SEC-07** (SHOULD) Access to health records is logged. Every read and change of a person's health record by staff or professionals is logged with who, when and why, and the logs are reviewed.  
      Evidence:
